prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In Ocean's wide domains, Half buried in the sands, Lie skeletons in chains, With shackled feet and hands. Beyond the fall of dews, Deeper than plummet lies, Float ships, with all their crews, No more to sink nor rise. There the black Slave-ship swims, Freighted with human forms, Whose fettered, fleshless limbs Are not the sport of storms. These are the bones of Slaves; They gleam from the abyss; They cry, from yawning waves, "We are the Witnesses!" Within Earth's wide domains Are markets for men's lives; Their necks are galled with chains, Their wrists are cramped with gyves. Dead bodies, that the kite In deserts makes its prey; Murders, that with affright Scare school-boys from their play! All evil thoughts and deeds; Anger, and lust, and pride; The foulest, rankest weeds, That choke Life's groaning tide! These are the woes of Slaves; They glare from the abyss; They cry, from unknown graves, "We are the Witnesses!"

Across the ocean’s wide domains,  
Half-buried in the sands,  
Lie skeletons in chains,  
With shackled feet and hands.  

Beyond the reach of falling dews,  
Deeper than the plummet lies,  
Ships drift with all their crews,  
No more to sink or rise.  

There the black slave ship swims,  
Freighted with human forms,  
Whose fettered, fleshless limbs  
Are no longer the sport of storms.  

These are the bones of slaves;  
They gleam from the abyss.  
From yawning waves, they cry,  
“We are the Witnesses!”  

Within Earth’s wide domains  
Are markets for men’s lives;  
Their necks are galled by chains,  
Their wrists constricted by gyves.

In deserts makes its prey;  
Murders that, with fright,  
Drive schoolboys from their play!  

All evil thoughts and deeds—  
Anger, lust, and pride—  
The foulest, rankest weeds  
That choke Life’s groaning tide!  

These are the woes of slaves;  
They glare from the abyss.  
From unknown graves, they cry,  
“We are the Witnesses!”
outputs.L2:
Across the ocean’s vast expanse, skeletons lie partly covered by sand, iron restraints still fastening their hands and feet. Far below the reach of falling dew—deeper than any sounding weight can measure—ships drift with entire crews aboard, destined neither to descend nor surface again. A dark slave vessel moves there, laden with human remains; its prisoners’ shackled, fleshless arms and legs can no longer be tossed by storms. From the depths, the bones of enslaved people shine and call through the gaping waters: “We bear witness!”

Throughout the broad lands of Earth, human beings are bought and sold. Chains wound their necks, while iron fetters constrict their wrists. In deserts, kites feed upon corpses; murders are so horrifying that they frighten schoolchildren away from their games. Every wicked idea and act—rage, desire, and arrogance—grows like the vilest weeds, clogging the anguished current of life. These are the sufferings endured by enslaved people. From the abyss and from unmarked graves, they stare outward and proclaim: “We bear witness!”
outputs.L3:
The ocean conceals the chained skeletons of enslaved people who died aboard slave ships, many of which sank during the brutal transatlantic passage. Though their remains lie in the abyss, the dead rise symbolically to bear witness to the horrors they endured and to ensure that their suffering is not forgotten.

Across the world, human lives have been bought and sold, while enslaved people have suffered imprisonment, physical restraint, violence, and abuse. Slavery brings not only death and murder, but also terror, degradation, and profound moral corruption, destroying both its victims and the humanity of those who perpetuate it.

From unmarked graves and the darkest ocean depths, the enslaved dead continue to testify. Their silent presence stands as an enduring accusation against the cruelty and injustice inflicted upon them—and as a demand that history remember their lives, their suffering, and their humanity.
outputs.L4:
The poem offers a powerful condemnation of slavery and the transatlantic slave trade by confronting readers with the physical and spiritual remains of its victims. Images of chained skeletons and sunken slave ships reveal the terrible fate of those who were transported across the ocean under brutal and inhuman conditions. Human markets evoke the degradation of people who were treated as property, while unmarked graves symbolize the countless lives erased from official history. Together, these images transform the landscape and the sea into places of memory, haunted by suffering that cannot be buried or concealed.

The dead function as witnesses to the violence committed against them. Although they were denied freedom, dignity, and often even a proper burial, their remains continue to testify to what happened. Their silent presence becomes a form of accusation, exposing both the cruelty of individual acts and the moral corruption of the entire system that permitted human beings to be bought, sold, imprisoned, and killed for profit. The poem therefore presents slavery not merely as a historical institution but as a profound violation of humanity.

By allowing the victims to speak symbolically from ships, chains, markets, and graves, the poem resists attempts to minimize or forget their suffering. The past remains present, demanding acknowledgment and remembrance. Its haunting imagery insists that the victims cannot be reduced to statistics or erased from collective memory: their pain endures as evidence, and their voices continue to condemn the injustice that destroyed their lives.
outputs.L5:
The ocean kept every secret ever whispered into its waves.

Mara stood at the edge of the shore, holding the letter in one hand while the wind pulled at her coat. She had crossed half the world to learn the truth, only to discover that truth was rarely whole.

“I never stopped loving you,” the letter said.

It was not exactly a lie. But it left out the years of silence, the unanswered calls, and the life built with someone else. A half-truth, Mara realized, could be more dangerous than a lie because it still carried the shape of honesty.

She folded the letter and let it fall into the ocean.

The water accepted it without judgment, blurred the ink, and carried the words away.
